virtualThreads.title: Virtual Threads (Project Loom) & Carrier Unmounting
virtualThreads.subtitle: Visualize lightweight user-mode Virtual Threads mounted on ForkJoinPool Carrier OS Threads, and automatic unmounting during blocking socket/DB I/O.
virtualThreads.mentalModel: Virtual Threads decouple Java threads from OS threads — when a Virtual Thread blocks on I/O, the JVM unmounts it from the Carrier OS thread so the OS thread can immediately execute another Virtual Thread.

failureModes: Thread Pinning: Occurs when a Virtual Thread calls blocking I/O inside a `synchronized` block or native JNI method, preventing the JVM from unmounting it from the Carrier Thread.
Monolithic ThreadLocal Memory Leak: Spawning 100,000 Virtual Threads with large `ThreadLocal` allocations will consume gigabytes of heap memory.
tradeOffs: Virtual Threads vs Reactive Programming (WebFlux): Virtual Threads allow writing standard imperative blocking code (`Thread.sleep()`, JDBC) while achieving reactive-level throughput without callback hell or Mono/Flux complexity.
theoryData.productionScenario: An enterprise payment gateway operating 200 platform threads hit 100% CPU and socket exhaustion at 500 RPS. Migrating to Java 21 Virtual Threads (`Executors.newVirtualThreadPerTaskExecutor()`) allowed the system to serve 15,000 concurrent RPS using only 8 Carrier OS Threads.

interviewQA.q: What is Virtual Thread Pinning and how do you resolve it?
interviewQA.a: Pinning happens when a Virtual Thread cannot be unmounted from its Carrier OS Thread during blocking I/O because it is executing inside a `synchronized` block/method. Fix it by replacing `synchronized` with `java.util.concurrent.locks.ReentrantLock`.

quizData.question: Should you pool Virtual Threads using a fixed ThreadPoolExecutor (`newFixedThreadPool`)?
quizData.answer: NO! Virtual Threads are extremely cheap (~1KB memory footprint) and intended to be created per-task and discarded. Pooling virtual threads limits concurrency and reintroduces resource contention bottlenecks.

threadPool.title: ThreadPoolExecutor Internals & Rejection Policies
threadPool.subtitle: Visualize task submission flow: Core Threads → Work Queue → Max Threads → Rejection Policy (Abort, CallerRuns, Discard, DiscardOldest).
threadPool.mentalModel: ThreadPoolExecutor processes tasks with Core Threads first; when busy, tasks buffer in the Work Queue; when queue fills, it spawns up to Max Threads; when full, Rejection Policy triggers.

failureModes: Unbounded Queue OOM: Using `Executors.newFixedThreadPool(n)` uses an unbounded `LinkedBlockingQueue` (Integer.MAX_VALUE), which accumulates tasks under load until Java Heap OOM occurs.
Thread Starvation Deadlock: Submitting tasks that wait for other tasks submitted to the same fixed thread pool can cause complete deadlock.
tradeOffs: CallerRunsPolicy vs AbortPolicy: `CallerRunsPolicy` degrades throughput gracefully by forcing the submitting thread (e.g. Tomcat HTTP thread) to run the task, providing natural backpressure; `AbortPolicy` throws `RejectedExecutionException` immediately.
theoryData.productionScenario: During a black Friday traffic spike, an asynchronous log exporter flooded its thread pool. Because it used `AbortPolicy`, thousands of order requests failed with `RejectedExecutionException`. Switching to `CallerRunsPolicy` throttled incoming HTTP requests safely without dropping orders.

interviewQA.q: What is the exact order ThreadPoolExecutor follows when a new task is submitted?
interviewQA.a:
1. If active threads < corePoolSize, spawn new core thread to run task.
2. Else if work queue is not full, add task to work queue.
3. Else if active threads < maximumPoolSize, spawn new non-core thread.
4. Else execute Rejection Execution Handler policy.

quizData.question: Why does `Executors.newCachedThreadPool()` risk server crash under heavy load?
quizData.answer: `newCachedThreadPool()` sets core size to 0, max size to `Integer.MAX_VALUE`, and queue to `SynchronousQueue`. Under heavy traffic spikes, it will spawn thousands of OS threads, exhausting server native memory and CPU context-switching capacity.
